title: GOD SAID THEY COULD NOT ENTER FOR TEN GENERATIONS… SO HOW DID JESUS OPEN THE DOOR?
paragraphs: GOD SAID THEY COULD NOT ENTER FOR TEN GENERATIONS… SO HOW DID JESUS OPEN THE DOOR?
The disturbing law of Deuteronomy 23:2, the Hebrew word most Christians misunderstand, and the breathtaking Gospel truth that your family’s shame does not have to become your eternal identity.
What if you discovered that something that happened before you were born could affect where you belonged for ten generations?
Not something you did.
Not a sin you committed.
Not a decision you made.
Something connected to the circumstances of your birth.

Imagine growing up knowing that your parents' story carried a stigma you could never erase. Imagine watching other families participate in sacred community life while wondering whether there would ever be a place for yours.
Now imagine opening your Bible and finding these words:
“A bastard shall not enter into the congregation of the LORD; even to his tenth generation shall he not enter into the congregation of the LORD.” — Deuteronomy 23:2 (KJV)
There it is.
A verse that can make even a devoted Christian stop reading.
Ten generations.
Not ten days of repentance.
Not ten years of waiting.
Ten generations.
And suddenly, questions begin rising from places we rarely allow anyone to see.
Why would God establish such a restriction?
What did the child do wrong?
Does the shame of a family follow its descendants?
And if this was written in God's law, what does it mean when the same Bible tells us that Jesus Christ came to welcome sinners, restore the broken, and bring outsiders near?
Stay with this.
Because the answer is not found by pretending that Deuteronomy 23:2 was never written.
It is found by understanding what God actually said, what the ancient law meant, and how the unfolding story of Scripture leads us to Jesus Christ.
And somewhere in that story, you may recognize your own.
Perhaps you were born into a family that people whispered about.
Perhaps your parents never married.
Perhaps your father disappeared before you learned how to pronounce his name.
Perhaps you grew up carrying the consequences of another person's choices.
Or perhaps your story is different, but the wound feels familiar.
You have spent years trying to prove that you deserve to belong.
And the question beneath all those years has never really changed.
Is there a place for someone like me?
Before we answer, we must listen carefully to the Scripture itself.
The Hebrew text of Deuteronomy 23:2 reads:
לֹא־יָבֹא מַמְזֵר בִּקְהַל יְהוָה גַּם דּוֹר עֲשִׂירִי לֹא־יָבֹא לוֹ בִּקְהַל יְהוָה׃
Lo-yavo mamzer biqhal Adonai; gam dor asiri lo-yavo lo biqhal Adonai.
A close English rendering is:
“A mamzer shall not enter the assembly of the LORD; even the tenth generation belonging to him shall not enter the assembly of the LORD.”
The pronunciation above uses Adonai as the traditional spoken substitute for the divine name represented by the four Hebrew letters יהוה.
Now notice something important.
The Hebrew word translated “bastard” in the King James Version is מַמְזֵר — mamzer.
And understanding that word changes how we approach the passage.
In modern English, “bastard” is often understood as a child born to unmarried parents. It is also frequently used as an insult.
But we cannot simply take a modern English definition, carry it thousands of years backward, and assume that it captures the meaning of ancient Hebrew law.
The precise biblical scope of mamzer is debated.
The word appears only twice in the Hebrew Bible: here in Deuteronomy 23:2 and in Zechariah 9:6, where its meaning is also disputed.

Later Jewish legal tradition developed a more specific definition. In Mishnah Yevamot 4:13, the category is associated with offspring from certain prohibited sexual relationships, although the precise boundaries are discussed among the rabbis.
That later interpretation is important historical evidence, but we should not pretend that every detail of later rabbinic law is explicitly stated in Deuteronomy itself.
Some modern translations use expressions such as “one of illegitimate birth,” while others emphasize a forbidden union.
These are attempts to communicate a difficult ancient term.
What we can say confidently is that the Hebrew word does not justify declaring that every child born to unmarried parents is personally cursed, spiritually inferior, or rejected by God.
Scripture does not give us permission to place that burden on children.
And that matters more than some people realize.
Because there are people sitting in churches today who have spent their entire lives feeling like an apology for a decision they never made.
They hear sermons about purity, marriage, family, and righteousness.
Those teachings matter.
God's design for sexual faithfulness and marriage is not something we should dismiss.
But somewhere along the way, some have confused the moral responsibility of parents with the personal worth of their children.
Those are not the same thing.
A child is not an immoral act.
A child is a human being made in the image of God.
And we must never turn a biblical warning about sin into a weapon against someone who did not commit it.
But that still leaves us with the troubling restriction.
What did it mean to be excluded from the “assembly of the LORD”?
The Hebrew expression is קְהַל יְהוָה — qehal YHWH, the assembly or congregation of the LORD.

Its exact institutional meaning in Deuteronomy 23 has been debated. Interpreters have connected it with formal membership in Israel's covenant community, public religious participation, or particular communal privileges.
It would be too simplistic to assume that it necessarily meant a person could never pray, seek God's mercy, or worship in any sense.
The text establishes a serious boundary within ancient Israel's covenant order, but it does not explicitly answer every question about an individual's spiritual relationship with God.
And we must remember where this command appears.
Israel was not a modern nation operating under a secular constitution.
It was a covenant people whose religious, communal, and legal identity was bound to God's commands.
Deuteronomy 23 contains several regulations about participation in the assembly. These reflect boundaries belonging to that particular historical covenant setting.
The law was real.
Its consequences were serious.
And we do not honor Scripture by erasing the difficulty.
But neither do we honor Scripture by lifting an ancient covenant restriction out of its context and using it to pronounce eternal condemnation on people today.
A restriction concerning ancient Israel's assembly is not the same thing as a declaration that a person's soul can never receive God's grace.
Those are different claims.
And the Bible itself gives us reasons to distinguish them.
Listen to what God says through the prophet Ezekiel:
“The soul that sinneth, it shall die. The son shall not bear the iniquity of the father, neither shall the father bear the iniquity of the son.” — Ezekiel 18:20 (KJV)
Read that again.
“The son shall not bear the iniquity of the father.”
This does not mean that the consequences of sin never affect later generations.
They often do.
An alcoholic father's choices can leave wounds in his children.
An unfaithful spouse can fracture an entire household.
Abuse, abandonment, deception, and violence can shape lives long after the original act.
Sin can leave consequences that children never chose.
But experiencing the consequences of another person's wrongdoing is not the same as bearing personal guilt for that wrongdoing.
Ezekiel insists that God judges persons justly.
And that truth should make every parent, pastor, teacher, and Christian community think carefully about the labels they place on children.
Because sometimes the most painful rejection does not come from strangers.
It comes from people who know the language of religion.
A child walks into a room.
Adults exchange glances.
Someone whispers about the parents.
Someone makes a joke about the family's history.
Someone says something cruel and then calls it biblical truth.
And the child learns a lesson no child should ever have to learn:
Some people have decided who I am before they even know me.
Years pass.
The child becomes an adult.
The adult becomes successful, responsible, hardworking, and respectable.
But somewhere inside, that old voice remains.
You don't belong.
And this is where we need to understand something about the Bible.
The Scriptures do not merely describe humanity's sin.
They also reveal God's unfolding purpose to redeem sinners and bring people near to Himself.
Consider what happens in Isaiah 56.
There, the LORD speaks about foreigners and eunuchs, people whose circumstances could place them outside certain privileges associated with Israel's earlier covenant regulations.
God declares:

“Neither let the son of the stranger, that hath joined himself to the LORD, speak, saying, The LORD hath utterly separated me from his people: neither let the eunuch say, Behold, I am a dry tree.” — Isaiah 56:3 (KJV)
Then comes an astonishing promise to faithful eunuchs:

“Even unto them will I give in mine house and within my walls a place and a name better than of sons and of daughters: I will give them an everlasting name, that shall not be cut off.” — Isaiah 56:5 (KJV)
Do you hear the tenderness?
Do not say that you are utterly separated.
Do not say that you are a dry tree.
Do not conclude that your future is empty.
The passage does not simply cancel every earlier law without explanation. It speaks prophetically of God's gracious purposes and of a future in which those who join themselves to Him are welcomed.
Isaiah 56 does not specifically mention the mamzer of Deuteronomy 23:2.
We should be careful not to claim that it does.
But it reveals something beautiful about the direction of God's redemptive promise.
The God who is holy is also the God who promises to gather people who once stood at the margins.
And then, centuries later, Jesus Christ came.
Not as a religious celebrity looking for the approval of respectable people.
Not as a teacher who only welcomed those with flawless family histories.
He came as the promised Messiah.
The eternal Son of God took on human flesh.
And when He entered the world, He did not arrive in a story free from suspicion, suffering, or scandal.
Matthew tells us that Mary was found to be pregnant through the Holy Spirit before she and Joseph came together as husband and wife.
Joseph initially considered ending the betrothal quietly.
Then an angel told him:
“Joseph, thou son of David, fear not to take unto thee Mary thy wife: for that which is conceived in her is of the Holy Ghost.” — Matthew 1:20 (KJV)
This matters.
Jesus was not conceived through an illicit human relationship.
The Christian confession of His virginal conception must never be confused with a claim that He was the offspring of a forbidden sexual union.
He was conceived by the Holy Spirit.
He was and is the sinless Son of God.
But the circumstances surrounding Mary's pregnancy could be misunderstood by people who did not know the truth.
And later, in John 8:41, during a heated dispute, Jesus' opponents say:
“We be not born of fornication.”
Some interpreters have understood this as a possible insinuation against Jesus' birth, while others understand it differently in the context of the argument.
The text does not establish beyond doubt that they were accusing Jesus of illegitimacy.
Yet it reminds us how quickly questions about ancestry and moral legitimacy could become weapons in a hostile conversation.
Jesus knew what it meant to face rejection.
John 1:11 says:
“He came unto his own, and his own received him not.”
And Isaiah 53:3 describes the suffering servant as:
“Despised and rejected of men; a man of sorrows, and acquainted with grief.”
The Savior who came to reconcile sinners to God was Himself rejected by many of the people He came to save.
Think about that.
The One through whom all things were made entered a world where human beings judged worth through ancestry, status, reputation, and outward appearances.
And He came to accomplish something none of us could accomplish for ourselves.
He came to save.
Now look at the genealogy of Jesus in Matthew chapter 1.
It is easy to rush through those names.
Abraham.
Isaac.
Jacob.
Judah.
Perez.
Boaz.
Obed.
Jesse.
David.
But stop at one particular detail.
Matthew 1:3 says:
“And Judas begat Phares and Zara of Thamar.”
In contemporary spelling, Judah fathered Perez and Zerah by Tamar.
That short line carries a painful and morally complicated history.
Genesis 38 tells the story of Judah and Tamar.
Tamar had been married to Judah's son Er, who died. Under the family obligations of that time, provision was supposed to be made for her future, but Judah failed to fulfill what he had promised.
Tamar eventually disguised herself, and Judah had sexual relations with her without knowing her identity.
She became pregnant.
When Judah learned of her pregnancy, he initially demanded punishment.
Then the truth came out.
He recognized the evidence that implicated him.
And Judah said:
“She hath been more righteous than I.” — Genesis 38:26 (KJV)
What a moment.
The man prepared to condemn her was confronted with his own wrongdoing.
The man who wanted judgment had to acknowledge his own failure.
And from that morally tangled family history came Perez.
Perez became an ancestor of King David.
And Matthew deliberately includes him in the recorded genealogy of Jesus Christ.
We need to be precise here.
Scripture does not explicitly identify Perez as a mamzer under Deuteronomy 23:2, nor does it say that Jesus' genealogy proves a particular legal exception to that verse.
Genesis 38 happened before the giving of the Mosaic law, and the relationship between later legal categories and this earlier narrative should not be assumed.
But the theological significance remains powerful.
God did not conceal the failures and complications of the family line through which the Messiah would come.
The genealogy contains real human beings.
Not polished legends.
Not people whose lives were untouched by sin.
Real people with histories that could make respectable society uncomfortable.
And God's redemptive purpose continued through that history.
This is not God approving Judah's wrongdoing.
This is God demonstrating that human sin cannot overthrow His sovereign purpose.
And then there is Ruth.
A Moabite woman.
A widow.
A foreigner who left her homeland and joined herself to Naomi and Naomi's people.
Ruth said:
“Thy people shall be my people, and thy God my God.” — Ruth 1:16 (KJV)
That declaration was not a magical formula.
It expressed allegiance, loyalty, and a turning toward the God of Israel.
And Ruth became the great-grandmother of David.
Matthew 1:5 names her in the genealogy of Jesus.
Why is that significant?
Because Deuteronomy 23:3 also places restrictions on Ammonites and Moabites entering the assembly of the LORD, using language extending even to the tenth generation.
Ruth's presence in the messianic family line has therefore prompted generations of readers to wrestle with the relationship between the law, the story of Ruth, and God's gracious purposes.
Jewish interpretation has traditionally distinguished Moabite men from Moabite women in applying this prohibition, while Christian interpreters have approached the relationship in various ways.
We should not pretend that every historical and legal question is simple.
But we should not miss what Scripture unmistakably tells us.
Ruth trusted the God of Israel.
She was received into a family.
Her story became part of the ancestry of David and, ultimately, the Messiah.
A foreign widow who once stood outside Israel by birth became part of one of the most extraordinary family stories in the Bible.
And then we reach the New Testament's breathtaking announcement.
The saving work of Jesus Christ brings believing Jews and Gentiles into one people of God.
Paul writes to Gentile believers in Ephesians 2.
He reminds them that they had once been:
“Aliens from the commonwealth of Israel, and strangers from the covenants of promise, having no hope, and without God in the world.” — Ephesians 2:12 (KJV)
That is a devastating description.
Strangers.
Separated.
Without hope.
Without God.
But the next verse begins with two words that change everything.
“But now.”
“But now in Christ Jesus ye who sometimes were far off are made nigh by the blood of Christ.” — Ephesians 2:13 (KJV)
Far off.
Made near.
Not through a fabricated family history.
Not through pretending sin never happened.
Not through purchasing acceptance.
Not through becoming socially impressive.
Through the blood of Jesus Christ.
And Paul continues:
“For he is our peace, who hath made both one, and hath broken down the middle wall of partition between us.” — Ephesians 2:14 (KJV)
In context, Paul is speaking particularly about the reconciliation of Jews and Gentiles through Christ.
He is not giving a technical commentary on the meaning of mamzer in Deuteronomy 23:2.
But his teaching reveals the magnificent reality of the new covenant.
Access to God through Christ is not restricted to people who possess the right ethnic pedigree or social standing.
Through faith in the crucified and risen Savior, people who were once far away are brought near.
And here is where this ancient passage becomes intensely personal.
Maybe nobody has ever called you a mamzer.
Maybe nobody has quoted Deuteronomy 23:2 against you.
But you know what it feels like to be the person standing outside.
You know what it feels like to see other people welcomed while you quietly wonder whether your history disqualifies you.
You know what it feels like to sit in church, sing the songs, bow your head, and still wonder whether God sees the things you are ashamed to mention.
Maybe the scandal was not your birth.
Maybe it was your divorce.
Your addiction.
Your abortion.
Your infidelity.
Your years of rebellion.
Your secret pornography.
Your abandoned responsibilities.
Your dishonesty.
Your bitterness.
Your pride.
Your double life.
Or perhaps it was something done to you.
Something you never chose.
Something you have carried so long that you no longer remember who you were before it happened.
Please hear this distinction.
When we are guilty of sin, God calls us to repentance.
When we have been sinned against, we do not need to repent for the evil another person committed against us.
And when our story contains both our own wrongdoing and wounds inflicted by others, we need the wisdom to distinguish them.
The Gospel does not tell the wounded to accept blame for their wounds.
And it does not tell the guilty to excuse their sins.
It tells the truth about both.
We have all sinned and fallen short of God's glory.
We cannot save ourselves.
We cannot rewrite our past through human effort.
We cannot purchase forgiveness.
But God, in His mercy, sent His Son.
Jesus lived the sinless life we could not live.
He died for our sins.
He rose again.
And everyone who repents and trusts in Him receives forgiveness and eternal life.
That is not sentimental optimism.
That is the Gospel.
And it is more powerful than any human label.
Consider the Greek words of John 1:12:
ὅσοι δὲ ἔλαβον αὐτόν, ἔδωκεν αὐτοῖς ἐξουσίαν τέκνα θεοῦ γενέσθαι
Hosoi de elabon auton, edōken autois exousian tekna theou genesthai.
“But as many as received him, to them gave he power to become the sons of God.” — John 1:12 (KJV)
The Greek word τέκνα — tekna means children.
And ἐξουσία — exousia conveys authority or the right granted.
The promise is not that everyone automatically becomes God's child in the saving sense simply by existing.
John specifically speaks of those who receive Christ, those who believe in His name.
And John 1:13 makes clear that this new birth is not grounded in ordinary human ancestry.
It is of God.
Do you see the beauty?
Your earthly family history may explain much about where you came from.
But it does not have the power to prevent God from giving you new life in Christ.
You may have been unwanted by a parent.
You may have been rejected by a spouse.
You may have been shamed by a community.
You may have been treated as though your life began with an unforgivable mistake.
But when you come to Christ in repentance and faith, your standing before God rests on His grace, not on the reputation of your ancestors.
And the Apostle Paul says something even more extraordinary.
“Therefore if any man be in Christ, he is a new creature: old things are passed away; behold, all things are become new.” — 2 Corinthians 5:17 (KJV)
The Greek expression is:
καινὴ κτίσις — kainē ktisis
A new creation.
Not merely a better reputation.
Not simply a cleaned-up public image.
A new creation.
This does not mean every consequence of the past disappears overnight.
Some broken relationships require years of repair.
Some sins demand restitution.
Some wounds require patient healing.
Some painful memories remain.
Following Jesus does not erase responsibility.
But it changes the deepest question of identity.
You are no longer required to build your hope on proving that your past was perfect.
Your hope is Jesus Christ.
And now I want you to imagine a scene.
A person stands outside a great doorway.
For years, that person has believed there is no place inside.
Every memory seems to confirm it.
Every rejection.
Every insult.
Every failure.
Every whispered accusation.
The person has stopped knocking.
Not because the longing disappeared.
But because rejection became familiar.
Then someone approaches.
Not another accuser.
Not another religious spectator.
Jesus.
The One who knows the entire truth.
Not only the parts that can be explained.
The entire truth.
He knows the sins.
The wounds.
The secrets.
The fears.
The prayers you were too ashamed to speak aloud.
And He does not offer a lie to make you feel better.
He calls you to Himself.
To repentance.
To faith.
To a new life under His lordship.
That imagined scene is not a quotation from Deuteronomy or a promise that every earthly door will open.
It is a picture of the invitation Jesus truly gives.
“Come unto me, all ye that labour and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest.” — Matthew 11:28 (KJV)
And He says:
“Him that cometh to me I will in no wise cast out.” — John 6:37 (KJV)
Read that last promise slowly.
“I will in no wise cast out.”
Not because your sin is small.
Not because your story is respectable.
Not because you have earned admission.
But because Jesus is a sufficient Savior.
He does not save us by declaring sin harmless.
He saves us by bearing sin's judgment at the cross.
He does not call us to remain enslaved to the darkness.
He calls us out of it.
Grace is not permission to keep destroying ourselves.
Grace is God's undeserved favor that brings salvation and teaches us to turn away from ungodliness.
And if you have been hiding behind your family history, your religious performance, or your own shame, perhaps today is the day to stop running.
Not from the truth.
Toward Christ.
Because you cannot repent of what you refuse to acknowledge.
And you cannot heal by continually pretending the wound does not exist.
Some of you reading this have been Christians for years.
You know the verses.
You know the worship songs.
You know when to say amen.
But there is still a room inside your heart you have never opened honestly before God.
A room filled with things you wish were not part of your story.
You believe Jesus forgives sinners.
You simply struggle to believe His grace can reach you.
And perhaps the most difficult thing you need to hear today is this:
Your shame is not more powerful than the blood of Jesus.
Not your family's shame.
Not your personal failures.
Not the sins you have confessed a hundred times.
Not the labels other people refuse to stop using.
If you are in Christ, your ultimate identity is not the worst thing you have done or the worst thing that has been done to you.
Your identity is anchored in the Savior who died and rose again.
Romans 8:1 declares:
“There is therefore now no condemnation to them which are in Christ Jesus.”
That is not a promise of no consequences.
It is a promise concerning condemnation before God for those who belong to Christ.
And that distinction is everything.
The Gospel does not promise that every person will understand your story.
It does not promise that every broken family will reconcile.
It does not promise that every earthly institution will welcome you.
But it does promise that those who belong to Jesus Christ are reconciled to God.
And no human accusation can overturn the saving verdict of God.
So when we return to Deuteronomy 23:2, we should not return as careless readers who simply declare that the Old Testament no longer matters.
We return with reverence.
We acknowledge that the ancient law was part of Israel's covenant life.
We admit that some details of its application remain difficult.
We refuse to impose unsupported definitions on the Hebrew text.
We distinguish covenant-community restrictions from eternal salvation.
And we read the passage within the larger biblical story that culminates in Jesus Christ.
The law reveals the seriousness of holiness and covenant identity.
The prophets announce God's purposes of restoration and gathering.
The Gospel announces the saving work of Christ.
And the apostles proclaim that through Him, believing Jews and Gentiles have access to the Father by one Spirit.
This is not a story of God changing from cruel to kind.
It is the unfolding revelation of the one holy, just, merciful God accomplishing His redemptive purpose through Jesus Christ.
The same God who judges sin provides the Savior.
The same God who commands holiness extends mercy to repentant sinners.
And the same Scripture that records painful boundaries also announces the glorious hope of reconciliation through Christ.
Now think of the people who need to hear that.
The young woman who believes her past makes her unworthy of love.
The man who grew up without a father and still carries the wound.
The child who has been treated differently because of the circumstances of birth.
The believer who has fallen and wonders whether repentance is still possible.
The person who has never entered a church because they are convinced Christians would only judge them.
The exhausted mother praying that her children will not repeat her mistakes.
The father who wishes he could undo years of absence.
The Christian who appears strong in public but privately feels disqualified.
They do not need us to distort the Bible to comfort them.
They need us to tell them the truth about Jesus.
And perhaps someone you know is one conversation away from hearing that truth for the first time.
Not simply because a post deserves more attention.
But because there may be someone quietly reading your timeline who would never admit how desperately they need to hear that grace is still available.
Return to it when old accusations become loud again.
Return to the Scriptures.
Examine the passages yourself.
Let the Word of God, not the opinions of strangers, shape what you believe about holiness, repentance, and grace.
And I want to ask you something personal.
Not for a performance.
Not because you need to expose your deepest wounds publicly.
But because honest testimony can help another believer find the courage to seek Christ.
If you need prayer, you can simply comment, “Pray for me.”
And if you have a testimony of how Christ brought you out of a season of rejection, you are welcome to share what you feel comfortable sharing.
Someone else may recognize their own struggle in your words.
You never know whose faith may be strengthened by your testimony.
This is why Gospel Warrior exists.
Not to build a community around human personalities.
Not to turn painful stories into entertainment.
Not to replace your local church or the shepherding of faithful Christian leaders.
But to keep directing people back to Scripture, repentance, prayer, discipleship, and the transforming grace of Jesus Christ.
We want to reach the person who has never opened a Bible.
The believer whose faith has grown cold.
The Christian who is trying to rebuild after failure.
The parent praying over a struggling child.
The seeker who has questions they are afraid to ask.
And the wounded person who wonders whether God could ever welcome them.

It is voluntary financial support for the ongoing work of creating biblical teaching, devotionals, Gospel-centered articles, and discipleship resources that can encourage people to know and follow Jesus Christ.
But let me make something absolutely clear.
Scripture teaches:
“Every man according as he purposeth in his heart, so let him give; not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver.” — 2 Corinthians 9:7 (KJV)
God does not need financial pressure to accomplish His purposes.
The Gospel is free.
Salvation is God's gift.
And Christian generosity should be offered willingly, wisely, and with joy.
These resources and benefits are not the reason anyone should come to Jesus.
They are simply ways to support and participate in a growing ministry of biblical encouragement.
But if you believe in the mission and want to help sustain and expand it, we would be grateful to have you walk alongside us.
Keep opening your Bible.
Keep praying.
Keep gathering with faithful believers.
Keep turning away from sin.
Keep receiving God's grace with humility.
Perhaps someone in your family has drifted far from God.
Perhaps a friend has stopped attending church.
Perhaps someone you love has never understood what Jesus accomplished on the cross.
Not to win an argument.
Not to pressure them.
But to open a door for an honest conversation about the Savior.
Because the heart of this entire story is not a Hebrew legal category.
It is not a family scandal.
It is not even the painful number ten.
The heart of this story is Jesus Christ.
The Savior who entered our broken world.
The Lamb of God who takes away sin.
The crucified and risen Lord who calls sinners to repentance and faith.
And the One through whom those who were once far away can be brought near to God.
So let me leave you with one final question.
What if you have spent your entire life believing that the circumstances of your beginning have already determined the outcome of your eternity?
What if you have been listening to the wrong verdict?
What if the voice that keeps telling you that you are permanently disqualified is not the voice of Jesus?
Do not misunderstand.
You cannot save yourself by changing your story.
And you cannot enter God's kingdom merely by deciding that you deserve a place.
You need the Savior.
We all do.
But that Savior has already come.
He died.
He rose again.
And He calls you to repent, believe, and follow Him.
Your past may still need to be confronted.
Your sins may still need to be confessed.
Your relationships may still need to be repaired.
Your wounds may still need time, prayer, and wise care.
But none of those realities makes the mercy of Christ insufficient.
You are not saved by having a spotless family tree.
You are saved by grace through faith in Jesus Christ.
And if you belong to Him, you do not need to spend the rest of your life begging your past for permission to become who God has called you to be.
The world may remember the scandal that surrounded your beginning, but in Christ, that scandal does not have to write the final sentence of your story.
